Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input
tools.description: Set the value of a form element identified by `ref` (from read_page/find). Handles input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

value.description: The value to set. For checkboxes use boolean, for selects use option value or text, for other inputs use appropriate string/number

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this form fill does on the page and to what, for example 'Sets the delivery date to 29 September'. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__get_page_text
tools.description: Extract the visible text of the Browser pane's page (article/main content first, falls back to body innerText).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__javascript_tool
tools.description: Execute JavaScript in the Browser pane's page for DEBUGGING and INSPECTION only. Do NOT use this to implement UI changes — edit source code instead.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. Return values are serialized as JSON.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__navigate
tools.description: Navigate the Browser pane to a URL, or go "back"/"forward" in history. If the Browser pane isn't open yet, this opens it at the URL (no dev server needed).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

force.description: If the page shows a "Leave site?" dialog because of unsaved changes, discard those changes and navigate anyway. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_list
tools.description: List servers started with preview_start. Returns serverIds for use with other preview_* tools.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_logs
tools.description: Get server stdout/stderr output. Use to check for build errors, verify server behavior, or read debug output. Use 'level' to filter to errors only, or 'search' to filter for specific text. Use after preview_start.

level.description: Filter by level: 'all' (default) shows all output, 'error' shows only lines containing error/exception/failed/fatal

search.description: Filter to lines containing this text (e.g., '[DEBUG]', 'POST /api')

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_start

url.description: URL to open in the Browser pane without a dev server (instead of starting one by `name`).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_stop
tools.description: Stop a server started with preview_start.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_console_messages
tools.description: Get console output (log, info, warn, error, debug) from the Browser pane.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_network_requests
tools.description: List network requests, or fetch a specific response body by `requestId`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

urlPattern.description: Substring filter on the request URL as listed (auth values show as REDACTED).

requestId.description: If provided, returns the response body for this request instead of listing.

limit.description: Max entries to return when listing (default: 50).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_page
tools.description: Read the current page in the Browser pane as a YAML-style accessibility tree. Each interactive element is tagged `[ref_N]` for use with `computer`/`form_input`/`find`. Prefer this over screenshot for verifying text and structure. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default; if it exceeds the limit it is truncated with a note — pass a larger max_chars, or use ref_id/depth to focus.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

filter.description: 'interactive' returns only clickable/typable elements; 'all' (default) returns the full tree.

ref_id.description: Restrict the tree to descendants of this `ref_N` (from a previous read_page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_close
tools.description: Close one Browser pane tab. Closing the last tab closes the Browser pane itself (reopen it with `preview_start`).

tabId.description: Tab to close.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_context
tools.description: List every Browser pane tab (origin only — titles are page-authored). Returns {browserOpen, tabs: [{tabId, origin, isActive}]} plus a line saying whether the pane is currently displayed or hidden (a hidden pane still works, but its page runs as a background page, so timing and performance numbers from it can be off; prefer `read_page` / `get_page_text` over screenshots while it is hidden). browserOpen is false (and tabs empty) until `preview_start` or `navigate` opens the pane, so you don't need to call this before opening it.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_create
tools.description: Open a fresh blank Browser pane tab; returns the new tabId. Opens in the background by default — set `foreground: true` when the user wants to watch. Prefer `preview_start` with a `url` when you know the destination; use `navigate` to load a URL into a blank tab.

foreground.description: Front the new tab (user asked to see it or is following along). Default false: open behind the user's current tab.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_select

**Jev** is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first "System One" model. It is built to make fast, structured decisions for software rather than generate text for people. You send a *state* (your data as text or JSON) and typed *questions* about it. Jev evaluates each question in parallel and returns structured answers your code can use directly.

- **Choice:** picks an option from a list. Returns `choice`, `probabilities`, and `confidence`.
- **Score:** rates the state on a rubric. Returns `score`, `probabilities`, and `confidence`.
- **Noul:** answers whether a statement is true. Returns `noul`, a value from 0 to 1.

**Sentiment analysis:** The page does not mention sentiment analysis. It may be possible to approximate it with Score or Noul questions, but the page does not say so.

**API/SDK:** The page does not cover programming languages, SDKs, authentication, pricing, or rate limits. It describes only one request containing the state and questions, and one response containing the answers. The Quick Start page is linked for setup details, but its content was not provided.

input.prompt: Explain what 'confidence' means for jev: how computed, range, calibration, how it differs from probabilities.

toolu_01UtzvQKzeDBUJq4we41M5Cs.prompt: Explain what 'confidence' means for jev: how computed, range, calibration, how it differs from probabilities.

content.content:
The page doesn't mention "jev," so I'm assuming you mean TypeSafe's `confidence` property.

**What it is:** A single number from 0 to 1 that summarizes how concentrated an answer's `probabilities` are. TypeSafe returns it on every Choice and Score answer. Noul answers don't include it.

**How it's computed:**
- **Choice** (n options, p_max = top probability): (p_max − 1/n) / (1 − 1/n). Only the top probability counts. With three options, (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) and (0.6, 0.2, 0.2) both give 0.4.
- **Score** (ordered levels): it uses the probability-weighted distance from the most likely level, compared with the spread of an even distribution, floored at 0. Probability on a neighboring level lowers confidence less than probability on a distant level.
- **Noul** (no `confidence` field): the page suggests reading the probability directly, or using |2p − 1| if you want a similar scale.

**Range:** 0 to 1. It is 1 when all probability sits on one outcome and 0 when the probability is spread evenly (or, for Score, when the spread matches an even distribution).

**Calibration:** The page doesn't define or evaluate calibration. It recommends starting with conservative thresholds, testing with your own data, and adjusting, noting that "the correct threshold values depend on your domain and the performance of the model for your use case."

**Versus probabilities:** Probabilities give the likelihood of each option or level. Confidence is a derived summary of how sharp that distribution is, so it's a single value you can threshold on. It doesn't tell you which option is likely, only how decisive the model is. The page also notes that other measures, such as the top probability or the top-to-second ratio, can be computed from the same probabilities and may suit your application better.

content.content:
**Endpoint and auth**
- `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone`
- Headers: `Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>` and `Content-Type: application/json`
- Get an API key from the TypeSafe console.

**Request shape**
- `state`: the text or structured object to evaluate.
- `model`: a model ID, such as `jev-latest`.
- `questions`: an object mapping each question ID to a question definition:
  - Choice: `type: "choice"`, `instructions`, and `criteria` as an object of option labels to descriptions.
  - Score: `type: "score"`, `instructions`, and `criteria` as a list of rubric levels.
  - Noul: `type: "noul"` and `instructions`. It takes no criteria.

**Response shape**
- `model`: the model version that ran, such as `jev-1.13.0`.
- `answers`: one result per question ID, each with a `type`:
  - Choice: `choice`, `confidence`, and `probabilities`.
  - Score: `score`, `confidence`, `legend`, and `probabilities`.
  - Noul: `noul`, a value from 0 to 1.
- `usage`: `input_tokens` and `output_tokens`.

**SDKs and languages**
- Python: requires Python 3.10+. Install with `pip install typesafe-sdk`. The client reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the environment.
- JavaScript: requires Node.js 20+. Install with `npm install @typesafe-ai/sdk`.
- TypeScript: same package. Running `.ts` files directly requires Node.js 22.18+. The SDK infers answer types from your questions.
- Bash/curl: calls the endpoint directly and requires curl 7.76+.

**Not covered on this page**
- Rate limits, input size limits, and pricing are not specified.
- The page lists the Python and JavaScript retry policies and error handling only by link, without details.
- The page doesn't give a full list of model IDs. It names `jev-latest` and shows `jev-1.13.0` in a sample response.

# ADR-0002: Next.js (TypeScript) with PostgreSQL

## Context and problem statement
The brief names no mandatory stack ("Node / React, PostgreSQL, etc.") and asks for a runnable service with API and UI. The user first proposed a Tauri app with Rust and Astro. Tauri builds desktop apps, which conflicts with the `docker compose up` requirement, so the user reverted to the original Next.js stack.

## Decision drivers
- Runs under one `docker compose up` (Carma constraint, brief F9)
- Fit to a 7 to 9 hour budget; one language across API, worker and UI
- Typed SDKs exist for both enrichment providers (jev: `@typesafe-ai/sdk`, Node 20+)

## Considered options
1. Next.js (TypeScript), PostgreSQL, worker as a second process from the same codebase
2. Rust service + Astro frontend + PostgreSQL
3. Tauri desktop app

## Decision outcome
Chosen option: "Next.js (TypeScript) + PostgreSQL". Route handlers serve the API; a separate `worker` container runs the enrichment loop from the same repository. SQL is hand-written and parameterised (no ORM-built string interpolation).

### Consequences
- Good: one language and toolchain; fast to build; SDK types for jev.
- Bad: a framework that blends UI and API, so API boundaries need discipline; the worker is not a Next.js concern and must live outside route handlers.
- Risks: bundler and server-component defaults could leak server-only code to the client. Confirm with a build check (see devops spec).

### Confirmation
Compose brings up `db`, `app`, `worker`; the UI renders ids 6 and 18 safely (FP-6).

## Pros and cons of the options
1. Fast, typed, matches the brief; framework coupling.
2. Strong performance and safety; slower to build, more risk in the time budget.
3. Does not satisfy the runnable-service requirement.
EOF

# ADR-0003: Enrichment providers

## Context and problem statement
The brief asks for a summary, a sentiment class and 1 to 3 topics per article, with model choice justified on cost, quality and latency. The user will supply API keys and chose jev (TypeSafe) for sentiment and an OpenAI small model for summary and topics.

## Decision drivers
- P6 and P7: every derived value needs confidence, origin, method and range
- Cost at 50,000 articles a day
- Prompt-injection surface: untrusted text goes to both providers

## Considered options
1. jev (sentiment) + OpenAI small model (summary, topics)
2. One OpenAI call for all three
3. Mock only

## Decision outcome
Chosen option 1, behind a provider interface. A mock adapter stays for tests and for graders without keys (UNCONFIRMED: user to confirm; origin recorded as `mock`).

Facts from the jev docs (https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction, `/introduction/quickstart.md`, `/confidence.md`, read 2026-10-24):
- `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone`, Bearer key, body `{state, model, questions}`; model id `jev-latest` (response reports a version such as `jev-1.13.0`).
- A Choice question returns `choice`, `probabilities` and `confidence`. Confidence is 0 to 1 and summarises how concentrated the probabilities are: (p_max − 1/n) / (1 − 1/n). The docs do not claim it is calibrated.
- The docs do not state pricing, rate limits or input limits. These are unknowns for the cost analysis.

Mapping: sentiment is one Choice question over `positive | negative | neutral | mixed`. Stored per row: choice, per-class probabilities, raw confidence (0 to 1), range 0 to 1, normalised 0 to 100, origin `classifier_concentration`, model version from the response. This confidence means "how decisive", not "how likely to be right", and the UI must say so (P7).

Summary and topics: one call to the OpenAI model with structured output, topic enum from the controlled list (D4 default). The model id is not yet confirmed by the user (they said they would provide it). It is an environment setting, recorded per enrichment row, and the cost analysis stays blocked on it.

Confidence for summary and topics comes from the model's self-report, origin `llm_self_report`, never shown as a probability.

### Consequences
- Good: sentiment gets real probabilities; two providers show a deliberate cost/quality split in the README.
- Bad: two dependencies means two breakers, two budgets and two failure paths; an enrichment is only complete when both parts arrive. A job tracks the two parts separately so one outage does not block the other.
- Risks: jev pricing and limits unknown; its `mixed` class must be expressible in the rubric; text sent to two third parties.

### Confirmation
Tests FP-10 to FP-14 per provider; budget ledger per provider; cost analysis with real prices once known.
EOF

# ADR-0004: Confidence is stored and shown

## Context and problem statement
Carma requires confidence on sentiment, topic and summary (P6, P7). The brief does not ask for it.

## Considered options
1. Store and show confidence with origin and range
2. Omit and document as growth path

## Decision outcome
Chosen option 1. Each derived value stores normalised 0 to 100, raw value, min/max range, origin and method version. Missing confidence is shown as "no confidence available", never a default. Self-reported LLM numbers are labelled as such.

### Consequences
- Good: P6 to P8 satisfied; strong README story.
- Bad: extra columns and UI; confidence from jev is a concentration measure, so the tooltip must explain it.
EOF

# ADR-0005: Boolean search grammar defaults

## Context and problem statement
The brief fixes the operators (`AND`, `OR`, `AND NOT`, brackets, phrases, `*`) and says keywords are case-sensitive. It leaves precedence, bare adjacent terms and wildcard placement open.

## Considered options
1. Lenient: `AND` binds tighter than `OR`; adjacent bare terms are an implicit `AND`; a leading `NOT` is a parse error (only `AND NOT` negates); wildcard as suffix only
2. Strict: explicit operators and brackets everywhere

## Decision outcome
Chosen option 1. Lowercase `and`, `or`, `not` are ordinary terms. Parse errors return a clear message with the position. Query length, nesting depth and term count are capped (values set by carma-searchability).

### Consequences
- Good: forgiving for users; the index can always be used.
- Bad: implicit `AND` can hide a typo such as a missing `OR`; mitigated by showing the parsed query back to the user.
EOF

# carma-searchability

Search is the product's core job: data is prepared so that it can be found, and it will be searched constantly. A missed mention is the most damaging failure Carma has (P3), so this skill designs for recall first and speed second, then makes the cost of that choice visible.

Finding articles is half the job. Carma's reports also slice a set of articles into counts, shares, trends and rankings, and the reader has to be able to trust those numbers. The analytical layer is designed here too, because it decides what has to be stored and indexed at ingestion and cannot be retrofitted cheaply.

Read `references/carma-context.md` first for the principles, constraints and spec conventions. The Appendix at the end of this file is a checklist of the data points, grains and report patterns that analysis needs; use it as a checklist and extend it when the feature brings new report types.

## Inputs

Read the latest non-superseded `.specs/architect/NNNN-*.md` for this feature and the ADRs that reference it. You need: what is searched, by whom, how often, the data flow and states, and the failure and hot path registers (FP/HP). If there is no architect spec, ask the user to run carma-architect or, for a small request, run its analysis inline and say so.

First check applicability. If no requirement involves finding, filtering, matching or aggregating content, say that search design is not needed and stop. Do not invent a search problem.

## Workflow

### 1. Separate the three kinds of search

They look similar and have different cost profiles, so design them separately.

- **Ad hoc search.** An analyst types a query against the stored archive. Latency of seconds is fine, but queries are varied and frequent.
- **Standing queries.** Saved brand and keyword definitions that must be evaluated against every incoming article so mentions reach users within 15 minutes of `published_at` (P1). At 800 articles a second this is a reverse-search problem: the cost grows with the number of saved queries times arrivals. Matching at ingestion beats re-scanning the archive.
- **Analytical queries.** Report and dashboard questions: "what share of each market's coverage mentions X", "volume by month split by sentiment", "who was quoted most, and how negatively". They read many articles and return few numbers. Cost is driven by the number of articles in scope and the number of dimensions, so they are served from structures prepared at ingestion (step 7), not by scanning text.

For each, write down: who uses it, expected volume, acceptable latency, and the cost of a false negative versus a false positive. Carma's stated emphasis is not missing a mention, so false negatives cost more. Say so, then design for high recall with precision handled by ranking and review (P4), not by narrowing the match. For analytical queries the equivalent risk is a number that is wrong without looking wrong, so the cost to state is "a plausible but incorrect figure reaches a client".

Name the analytical questions the feature must answer. Take them from the requirements, and from the report patterns in the Appendix (section C). Each question later becomes a test (step 11).

### 2. Define the searchable document

List exactly what is indexed per article: `headline`, `body`, `source`, `published_at`, `language`, plus derived fields such as entities, topics and sentiment. For derived fields, carry their confidence and origin (P6, P7) so results can be filtered or ranked by them. State which fields are searched as text, which are filters, and which are only displayed.

Keep the extracted text as stored (raw markup is not retained by default). Normalised or tokenised forms are derived from it so they can be rebuilt when the method improves, and a result can always be traced to what was published (P8).

Headline and body are separate searchable fields. Some analysis is about the headline alone (emotive wording, "named in the headline"), and matching the body for those questions gives wrong answers.

### 3. Tokenization and normalisation, per language (P5)

The same data model must serve every language. Design a language-aware analysis step and a safe fallback, rather than special cases scattered through queries.

- **English and similar.** Case folding, stemming or lemmatisation, stop words. Decide whether brand names and short tokens (for example "AI") bypass stop words, because aggressive stop-word lists silently lose mentions.
- **Arabic.** Right-to-left. Normalise before indexing: strip diacritics and tatweel, unify alef and ya/alef maqsura variants, handle taa marbuta variation, and decide on light stemming. Prefixed articles and conjunctions attach to words, so a brand name inside a longer token must still match. Mixed Arabic and Latin text in one article is normal.
- **Chinese.** No spaces between words, so whitespace tokenisation finds nothing. Options: dictionary-based segmentation (accurate, needs a segmenter and a maintained dictionary, and brand names missing from it get split wrongly) or character n-grams (bigrams are a robust recall-first baseline, larger index). Simplified versus Traditional script variants may need conversion. Full-width and half-width forms need normalisation.
- **Any other language.** A documented fallback: Unicode normalisation (NFKC), case folding, and a language-agnostic tokenizer, with the article's `language` field and a detected language used to route it. State how the fallback behaves for scripts it cannot segment and how that shows up in coverage reporting.

Always apply one Unicode normalisation form consistently at index and query time. Mismatched normalisation is a classic reason a mention that is visibly there is not found.

Treat the `language` field as a claim, not a fact. Plan for a mismatch with the detected language and say what happens to those articles (still indexed, and flagged).

### 4. Entities, aliases and quotes

Brand and person mentions are the main thing Carma users search for and aggregate on, so entity handling is part of search, not an extra.

- **Entity resolution.** Each entity has a canonical id, a type (organisation, product, person, place), aliases per language, abbreviations, known misspellings, and links to parents and subsidiaries. Company and product are separate entities with a link (a product and its maker, a brand and its parent). Joint names ("A-B") must resolve to both. Expect spelling variants, abbreviations, two names for one organisation, and the same entity written differently in each language.
- **Match confidence (P6).** Resolution to an entity id carries a confidence and origin. Unresolved or low-confidence mentions stay findable by plain text; they are never dropped (P3).
- **Time-varying attributes.** Some entity facts change over time (a role, a status, a launch date). Store them with validity dates so "before launch" and "while CEO" can be asked.
- **Quotes as records.** A quote has its own text, speaker (entity), speaker role and type, polarity, topic, and span in the article. Quote text is searchable on its own. This is what allows "who was quoted most", "most negative speakers" and "what did X say about Y".

### 5. Indexing strategies on PostgreSQL

Present options with trade-offs and a recommendation, and check what the codebase and environment actually allow (version, extensions) before leaning on any of them. Candidates:

- Full-text search with `tsvector`/`tsquery` and GIN, using a text-search configuration per language where one exists and a `simple`-style configuration otherwise. Weigh storing the vector (fast query, bigger writes) versus computing it on the fly.
- Trigram matching (`pg_trgm`) for fuzzy names and misspellings; consider its fit for short strings and its index size.
- n-gram or bigram approaches for CJK where the built-in parser cannot segment.
- Extensions or an external search engine are possible but may not be allowed in Carma's environment. Name them as options for the user to rule in or out; do not assume them.

Indexing cost competes with ingestion throughput. Note where index maintenance sits on the write hot path and hand that concern to carma-dba explicitly.

### 6. Bucketing and partitioning

Bucketing exists so most queries touch a small slice of the data.

- **Time buckets** by `published_at` (hour or day) fit append-only data, allow cheap retention by dropping whole buckets, and match the recency bias of most queries. Consider hot, warm and cold tiers with different index richness: the newest bucket may carry lighter indexes so items become searchable sooner (P1), with fuller indexes built as it ages.
- **Language buckets** where analysis differs by language. Weigh the benefit of per-language indexes against the cost of cross-language queries.
- **Source buckets** only if source-scoped queries are common and the cardinality is manageable.
- **Standing-query buckets.** Group saved queries by shared terms so an incoming article is checked against a candidate set instead of every query: an inverted map from term to queries, or a multi-pattern matcher, followed by verification of the candidates.

For each bucketing choice state the query patterns it helps, the ones it hurts (cross-bucket queries), and the operational cost.

### 7. Analytical layer: grains, facets and aggregates

This step makes reports possible. Work from the Appendix and from the analytical questions named in step 1.

**7a. Grains.** List the grains the feature needs (article, headline, entity mention, quote, attribute reference, tag, event, external observation) and for each the fields, whether it is multi-valued, and which fields are derived. One article produces many child records, so they are separate tables or partitions linked to the article by id, never columns or arrays on the article row when the analysis counts them. State the expected child records per article, because that multiplies write volume at 800 articles a second. Hand that figure to carma-dba.

**7b. Dimensions and measures.** For each question list the dimensions to group and filter by, and the measures (count at which grain, share of which base, score, rank, trend). For every share, write the numerator, the denominator and the grain of each. If a question cannot name its denominator, it is not yet well defined: raise it as a decision.

**7c. Vocabularies and groupings.** Topics, concerns, attributes, commentator types and similar sets are controlled vocabularies: versioned data with labels per language, not code. Every coded value stores the vocabulary version. Region groupings are named, versioned sets of markets and may overlap; one market can sit in several groups.

**7d. Scope.** A scope is a saved, versioned definition: markets, outlets or tiers, interval (half-open, with a stated time zone rule), topic query, and whether it covers the full population or a sample. Every aggregate and every report cites its scope id. The same scope on the same data and vocabulary versions must give the same number.

**7e. How aggregates are served.** Present options with trade-offs and a recommendation:
- Compute on demand from the child records, using partition pruning and covering indexes. Simple and always exact; slow when scopes are large.
- Incremental rollups maintained at ingestion at the finest grain needed (for example day by market by entity by category by polarity), then rolled up for coarser views. Fast; adds write cost and a reconciliation need.
- Materialised views refreshed on a schedule. Cheap to build; stale between refreshes, so staleness must be shown.
- Extensions or an external column store. Name as options for the user to rule in or out.

Pick per question, not globally. Rollups must be rebuildable from the child records so a corrected coder or vocabulary can be re-applied (P8). Hand rollup maintenance cost to carma-dba and its reconciliation to carma-backend-testing.

**7f. Drill-through invariant.** Every aggregate must be turnable into the list of records that produced it, and the list size equals the count. Rollups therefore keep the keys or the scope needed to regenerate the list. Say how this works for each rollup (P8).

**7g. Honest numbers.** Design these in, do not leave them to the interface:
- Carry the base count (n) with every rate. Flag low n; do not hide small groups (P3).
- Carry enrichment coverage: of the articles in scope, how many have the coded field computed, and how many are low confidence or unresolved. A share computed over 40% of the scope must say so (P3, P6).
- Say whether numbers come from the full population or a sample.
- Store the comparison set and tie rule with every rank.
- Keep positive and negative counts separate; do not store only a signed net.
- Say what a score is about and its scale: sentiment toward a stated proposition versus general tone, with min, max and the meaning of the midpoint (P7).

**7h. External series and events.** Survey results, search-interest indexes and event annotations are stored apart from article data, labelled with source, market, term or question, wave or date, sample size and scale. Indexed series are comparable only within one pull. They join to article aggregates by market and time bucket; they never get written into article tables. Decide whether external data is in scope at all (decision for the user).

**7i. Time handling.** Choose the finest bucket needed (usually day), roll up to week and month, and state the time zone rule for month and day boundaries, because UTC and local boundaries put different articles in different buckets.

### 8. Ranking, relevance and confidence

Ranking must serve P4 (signal over volume) without hiding anything (P3). Combine text relevance, recency, and optionally source or entity weights. A relevance score from the database's ranking functions is not calibrated, so when it is shown it is expressed on the 0 to 100% scale with its origin and min/max range stated (P6, P7), and the interface can say "database text-rank score, uncalibrated". Never imply it is a probability.

Ranking entities in an analytical view (most quoted, highest share positive) is different from ranking articles; it follows rule 3 in the Appendix: state the comparison set, the minimum n, and the tie handling.

### 9. Deduplication and near-duplicates

Wire stories republished across outlets create near-duplicates. Cluster them (for example with content fingerprints) but keep every copy and the link between them. Collapsing in the results view is fine; deleting is not, because each source's copy is a distinct mention (P3, P8).

Decide, per analytical measure, whether duplicates count once or each time. A syndicated story in ten outlets is ten mentions but one story, and the report's number changes depending on the answer. State it in the measure's definition.

### 10. Freshness and coverage signalling

Search must tell the user the truth about what it can see. Design the index watermark (the `published_at` or ingest time up to which everything is searchable), per-language and per-source coverage, and the three distinct empty states: no match, not covered, not yet processed (P3). Define how the answer to "is this complete?" is computed.

Analytics adds a fourth state: **not yet enriched**. An article can be searchable before sentiment, entities or quotes are computed (P1), but aggregates over those fields only see enriched articles. Every aggregate reports its watermark and its enrichment coverage, so a number over a half-enriched hour is not read as final.

### 11. Recall, precision and aggregate evaluation plan

Without measurement, "high recall" is a hope. Specify a labelled evaluation set: planted mentions in English, Arabic and Chinese including inflected, prefixed, misspelled, transliterated and mixed-script variants, plus articles that should not match. Define target recall for standing queries, how it is measured per language, and how regressions are caught when a tokenizer or dictionary changes. This feeds carma-backend-testing.

Add, for the analytical layer:
- **Coded-field accuracy.** A human-coded gold set per coded field (sentiment, topic, concern, commentator type, emotive headline, entity resolution, attribute and polarity). Define agreement targets per field and per language, and who codes it. A human-coded sample of articles, as Carma analysts produce for reports, is the natural source.
- **Aggregate correctness.** Known-answer tests: seed a small corpus where every expected count, share and rank is known, and check the aggregates exactly. Check the drill-through invariant on every rollup.
- **Aggregate stability.** How far does a headline number move when the coder, vocabulary version or model changes? Report that sensitivity so a change is a decision, not a surprise.
- **Rollup reconciliation.** Rollups equal a recount from the child records, within a stated tolerance and lag.

### 12. Decisions to put to the user

Raise choices that need a human: precision versus recall at the margin, index size versus write speed, segmentation method for Chinese, whether extra extensions or an external engine are acceptable, how much staleness a search may tolerate. For the analytical layer, also: which analytical questions are in scope, how duplicates count, full population or sampled enrichment (cost versus coverage), what the sentiment scale means and its range, whether external series are in scope, the time zone rule, the minimum n before a rate is flagged, and which controlled vocabularies exist and who owns them. Use the protocol in the context file.

## Output

Write the spec with these sections:

1. **Summary and applicability**
2. **Search use cases** (ad hoc, standing and analytical: users, volume, latency, false-negative cost; the analytical questions named)
3. **Searchable document** (fields, roles, derived fields with confidence)
4. **Language analysis plan** (English, Arabic, Chinese, fallback; normalisation; language mismatch handling)
5. **Entities and quotes** (resolution, aliases, match confidence, quote records)
6. **Index strategy** (options, recommendation, environment checks)
7. **Bucketing and partitioning** (scheme, tiers, standing-query grouping)
8. **Analytical layer** (grains and child records per article, dimensions and measures with numerator and denominator, vocabularies and groupings, scope definition, how aggregates are served, drill-through invariant, honest-number rules, external series, time handling)
9. **Ranking and confidence presentation**
10. **Deduplication** (including how duplicates count in each measure)
11. **Freshness and coverage signalling** (including enrichment coverage)
12. **Recall, precision and aggregate evaluation plan**
13. **Risks and hot paths** (extend the architect FP/HP registers with `FP-S` and `HP-S` entries, same columns; include child-record write amplification and rollup maintenance)
14. **Handoff** (what carma-dba must implement, what carma-telemetry must measure, what carma-backend-testing must verify, what carma-ux must show)
15. **Decisions needed and open questions**

In the handoff, be specific for the analytical layer:
- carma-dba: child record tables and their rate per article, rollup tables and refresh, vocabulary and scope tables, external series tables, retention per grain.
- carma-telemetry: enrichment coverage per field, rollup lag, aggregate query latency, drill-through count mismatches.
- carma-backend-testing: known-answer aggregate tests, rollup reconciliation, coded-field accuracy against the gold set.
- carma-ux: show n, enrichment coverage, scope and comparison set next to every figure; drill-through from every bar and number; low-n flags.

## Persisting the work (when run inside a codebase)

Follow "Spec conventions" in the context file. Number with `python scripts/next_spec_number.py .specs/search`, write `.specs/search/NNNN-<feature-slug>.md` with `spec: carma-searchability` front matter and list the architect spec under `inputs`. Edit in place while `draft`. Do not write ADRs yourself: when the user decides a search-design question, tell them it should be recorded and suggest running carma-architect to codify it as an ADR in `.specs/architect/adrs/`.

If you are not in a codebase, deliver the output in the conversation and offer to save it.

## Appendix: analytical data points checklist

Use this to check that the design can answer typical Carma report questions. Examples are generic; replace them with the feature's own entities and vocabularies. In reports the coded fields are often produced by human analysts. In the PoC they are derived automatically, so each carries confidence and origin (P6, P7) and can be overridden by a person (P9).

### A. Grains: the units that get counted

One article can hold many mentions, quotes and references, so these are separate records linked to the article. A percentage is only meaningful when the grain of the numerator and the denominator is stated.

| Grain | Example measure | Why it is its own record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Article | Share of a market's coverage that mentions a theme | Base unit and the usual denominator. |
| Headline | Share of headlines that are emotive rather than factual | A property of the headline text; headline and body can disagree. |
| Entity mention | Articles mentioning a brand, with sentiment toward it | Many entities per article, each with its own sentiment. |
| Quote | Who was quoted, how negatively, about what | Each has a speaker, speaker type, polarity and topic. Many per article. |
| Attribute reference | Positive and negative references to a quality (such as competence) for one brand | Counts references, not articles; one article can hold several. |
| Topic or theme tag | Number of times a theme appeared | Multi-label per article. |
| Concern or issue tag | Share of articles with at least one concern | Multi-label; reported as "at least one". |
| Event annotation | A dated event that explains a peak | An annotation layer on the time axis, not an article attribute. |
| External observation | Search-interest index, survey wave result | Not article data; joined by market, time and term. |
| Scope | The saved definition of what a report covers | Makes a number reproducible. |

### B. Fields per grain

"Multi" means several values per record. "Derived" means produced by enrichment and carries confidence and origin.

- **Article and source:** market, outlet, outlet tier, language (stored and detected), `published_at` and its day, week and month buckets, article-level sentiment (derived; state what it is toward, its scale and its midpoint), in-scope flag, sample flag.
- **Headline:** emotive or factual (derived), entities named in the headline (multi).
- **Entity mention:** entity id, type, role, match confidence, per-entity sentiment (derived), time-varying attributes with validity dates, parent and subsidiary links, prominence (headline, lead, passing).
- **Quote:** text and span, speaker entity, speaker role, speaker type (for example government, expert, company, public), polarity (derived), topic (multi), the organisation the speaker represents.
- **Attribute reference:** attribute (from a configurable vocabulary), polarity, entity it is about, sub-issue (multi).
- **Tags:** theme and concern, from versioned vocabularies, with co-occurrence derivable.
- **External series and events:** value, market, term or question, date or wave, sample size, scale, source; event date, text, market or global.

### C. Report patterns and the query each needs

| Pattern | Query shape | Design consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Percent of each market's coverage featuring X | count(articles with X) / count(articles in market within scope) | The denominator is a defined, queryable set with its own count. |
| Distribution across categories by region | group by region and category, normalised within region | Regions are overlapping groupings. |
| Volume over time split by sentiment | time bucket by polarity | Time-bucketed aggregates must be cheap. |
| Top speakers by negative quotes | group by speaker where polarity is negative, order, limit N | Speakers are entities; quotes are records. |
| Entity scorecard | per entity: counts by attribute and polarity, by region and market | Cross-tab of three dimensions, with n shown. |
| Rank of entities by share positive | proportion within a stated comparison set | Store the set, the minimum n and the tie rule. |
| Coverage against an external series | two series on one time axis | Align buckets and time zones; keep external data separate. |
| Coverage against survey waves | article aggregate per wave window against a survey value | Wave windows are scope definitions. |
| A peak explained by an event | bucket totals with nearby events | Event layer keyed by date and market. |
| Show me the articles behind this number | any aggregate to its record list | Drill-through must always work (P8). |
| Find what a person said | quote text by speaker, topic, date | Quote text is full-text searchable on its own. |

### D. Rules

1. **Every number states its grain and its denominator**, and gives the base count.
2. **Small bases are shown, never hidden.** A high percentage on four references is flagged, not removed (P3).
3. **Ranks are relative to a stated set.** The same entity ranks differently among all entities and among a subset. Store the set and the tie handling.
4. **Aggregates drill through.** Every count can be turned into the records that produced it, and the list size equals the count (P8).
5. **Scope is a saved, versioned definition.** Markets, outlets or tiers, topic query, and a half-open interval with a stated time zone. Reports often state their period two different ways; design that ambiguity out.
6. **Say whether a figure covers the full population or a sample**, and report enrichment coverage next to it (P3, P6).
7. **Controlled vocabularies are versioned data with labels per language.** Store the vocabulary version on each coded value (P5, P7).
8. **Region groupings overlap.** One market can be in several named groups; do not force a hierarchy.
9. **Entities need alias and hierarchy handling in every language**, with a match confidence (P6). Unresolved mentions stay findable by text.
10. **A sentiment score is toward something.** Store what it is about, its scale, min, max and the meaning of the midpoint (P7).
11. **Polarity counts are stored separately.** Volume and proportion both matter, and a signed net hides volume.
12. **External series are stored apart and labelled.** An indexed series is comparable only within one pull. A survey result carries wave dates, sample size and question wording.
13. **Time grain matters.** Pre-compute the finest grain needed (usually day) and roll up; state the time zone rule for boundaries.
14. **Headline and body are separate searchable fields.**
